title: Blood lead changes during pregnancy and postpartum with calcium supplementation.
ehr_evidence: Blood and urine samples were obtained monthly during pregnancy and the postpregnancy period for ≥ 6 months. Environmental samples of 6-day duplicate diet, drinking water, house dust, gasoline, and ambient air were collected quarterly.
summary: Longitudinal study of blood lead changes and lead mobilization from bone during pregnancy and postpartum in immigrant women, evaluating the effect of calcium supplementation.
key_findings: Geometric mean blood lead at first sampling was 2.4 µg/dL (range, 1.4–6.5).
Hematocrit-corrected blood lead increased by 10 to 50% (geometric mean 25%) during the third trimester.
Postpartum blood lead increased by 30 to 95% (geometric mean 65%; n = 8) from the late pregnancy minimum.
Significant increases in lead isotopic ratios from late pregnancy minimum occurred in 3 of 8 subjects (p < 0.01).
Extra lead flux mobilized from bone during late pregnancy and postpartum ranged from 50 to 380 µg (geometric mean 145 µg).
Cord:maternal blood lead geometric mean ratio was 0.72 (range 0.55–0.93; r² = 0.93).

Calcium supplementation delayed the timing of blood lead increases to 6–8 months gestation and halved the extra bone flux compared to a low-calcium cohort, but provided limited benefit for lead toxicity during lactation.
population: pregnant and postpartum female immigrants to Australia (aged 19–32 years) and two nonpregnant controls
exposure_domain: lead exposure and mobilization from bone; calcium supplementation
limitations: small sample size (n=10 pregnant subjects, n=2 controls)
absence of a placebo control group
potential unmeasured acute lead exposure sources (e.g., dietary changes at ethnic events)
